analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin copays at $35 a month in commercial plans and speeds cheaper biosimilar insulin to market.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate Health Committee with bipartisan support on August 7, 2026, was reported with a substitute amendment, and now sits on the Senate calendar awaiting a floor vote that has not been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cap what insured patients pay out of pocket for insulin at $35 per month, with no deductible and no prior-authorization hoops, for every type and form of insulin their plan covers. It would make it harder for drug makers to use FDA petitions to delay generic and biosimilar competitors, and would fast-track review of biosimilar insulin where fewer than three competitors exist. It would also fund a five-year pilot in ten states to get insulin to uninsured people for no more than $35 a month, plus a national hotline and resource center to help uninsured people find assistance programs.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use insulin with job-based, individual-market, or retiree coverage, who would pay at most $35 per 30-day supply with no deductible for at least one product of every insulin type and form their plan covers. Uninsured people with diabetes in ten pilot states would get insulin for no more than $35 a month through health centers and pharmacies, and a national hotline and website would help uninsured people find manufacturer and other assistance programs. Patients generally would benefit from faster competition from biosimilar and generic insulin.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insulin users and uninsured people with diabetes

how_it_helps.text: Commercial plans, including employer plans under ERISA and the tax code, must cover 'selected insulin products' with no deductible and cost-sharing capped at $35 per 30-day supply; from 2028 the cap is the lesser of $35 or 25% of the insulin's net negotiated price, tying patient cost to the price after rebates.
Plans are barred from imposing prior authorization or other medical-management requirements on selected insulin products except when clinically justified for safety or reasonable quantity limits.

The bill rewrites FDA citizen-petition rules so that petitions filed mainly to delay generic or biosimilar approval are identified as such and referred to the Federal Trade Commission, and courts must dismiss lawsuits that bypass the petition process.

FDA may expedite development and review of a biosimilar when fewer than three biosimilars to the same reference insulin are licensed, including expedited facility reinspection and a post-licensure report on whether the product actually reached the market.

A five-year pilot awards grants to ten states with high uninsured and diabetes rates to provide insulin to uninsured individuals at no more than $35 per month through federally qualified health centers and retail pharmacies, authorized at $100 million for fiscal 2027.

A grant would fund a 24/7 hotline and website helping uninsured people enroll in manufacturer assistance programs and locate pharmacies and health centers, with conflict-of-interest standards barring the operator from being an insulin manufacturer.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers and individuals who fund their premiums would bear the gap between the $35 patient cap and the insulin's cost, and would face new coverage and compliance requirements. Pharmacy benefit managers lose discretion over insulin rebates and prior authorization on selected insulin products, and the original version would have required them to pass all insulin rebates through to health plans. Brand-name insulin makers would face faster biosimilar competition and pressure on net prices, though no cap on list prices. The federal pilot and hotline would be paid for by appropriations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, employers, PBMs, brand insulin makers

drawbacks.text: The cost of capping patient copays does not disappear: health plans and employers absorb the difference between what the patient pays and the insulin's price, which likely flows back into premiums for all enrollees, and the reported version does not require insulin list prices to come down.

In the version the committee reported, the $35 commercial cap and related protections start for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2028, a year later than in the bill as introduced, and the reported version drops the introduced requirement that PBMs pass 100% of insulin rebates through to health plans.

The uninsured pilot covers only ten states and depends on annual appropriations rather than guaranteed funding, and the assistance-program hotline largely routes uninsured patients into manufacturer-run programs instead of directly lowering prices.

Requiring coverage of one product of each insulin type and form, without prior authorization, adds coverage mandates and administrative work for health plans, including self-insured employer plans, whose sponsor would otherwise have faced the stated intent of Congress to find an offset for federal costs in the introduced version.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one in ten Americans who use insulin, a hard $35 cap with no deductible and no prior authorization is a substantial, immediate benefit, and the anti-delay and biosimilar provisions attack the root cause of high prices by speeding competition. The main honest objection is financing: because the bill caps what patients pay but not what the drug costs, plans and employers pick up the difference and may raise premiums for everyone, so some of the benefit is a shift rather than a saving. The competition provisions are where real price relief would come from over time, but they are slower. The committee substitute also gave up the strongest PBM-rebate provision and delayed the cap a year, which weakens the bill without changing its direction.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee reported the bill favorably with a substitute amendment on August 7, 2026, placing it on the Senate calendar, but no floor vote has been scheduled and the Congress ends January 3, 2027.

narrative.text: Senator Jeanne Shaheen introduced the bill on March 25, 2026 together with 28 other senators from both parties, including Senator Susan Collins of Maine as a lead Republican.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.

On July 22, 2026 the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and on August 7, 2026 Chairman Bill Cassidy reported it; it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 552.

The committee substitute pushed the commercial cost-sharing cap from 2027 to plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2028, and dropped the introduced version's requirement that pharmacy benefit managers remit 100% of insulin rebates to health plans, while keeping the $35 cap, the anti-delay FDA petition reforms, the biosimilar expedited review, the ten-state uninsured pilot, and the hotline.
The introduced version had included a sense of Congress that any federal costs of the bill should be offset by later legislation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet: the bill is alive on the Senate calendar and insulin users would gain only if it becomes law. Under the status quo it preserves, brand insulin makers and PBMs keep operating under current rebate and pricing arrangements, with no floor vote taken away from anyone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand insulin makers and PBMs, so far

sides.party_line_note: Twenty-nine senators introduced the bill together across party lines, the 28 additional cosponsors split 14 Republicans, 13 Democrats, and 1 independent, and a Republican committee chairman reported it favorably; no one has publicly opposed it in the record.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: Plans must cover selected insulin products with no deductible, a $35 cap, and no prior authorization, absorbing the difference between the patient's copay and the drug's cost, which is likely passed to premiums. The mandate directly protects patients at the plan's expense, though large plans can spread the cost across all enrollees.

The bill bars plans from paying PBMs more than the capped amount for selected insulin products and limits PBM-run prior authorization, and the introduced version would have forced PBM and insurer rebate pass-through to plans; the committee substitute dropped the pass-through requirement, leaving the rebate system intact. PBM insulin revenue depends on opaque rebate flows that raise what patients ultimately pay.

Faster biosimilar competition, FTC referral of delay petitions, and copays tied to net-after-rebate prices squeeze their insulin franchise, but the bill never caps list prices and the substitute kept the rebate system, while the hotline and pilot steer uninsured patients into manufacturer assistance programs. Their pricing has kept insulin among the most expensive maintenance drugs for insured and uninsured patients alike.

The bill speeds FDA review for biosimilars where fewer than three exist and closes citizen-petition delay tactics, opening the insulin market to cheaper copies. Cheaper competition is what would bring sustained price relief to patients.

industries.industry: Federally qualified health centers and retail community pharmacies
industries.note: The ten-state pilot directs grants through health centers and community pharmacies to dispense low-cost insulin and allows expansion of health-center pharmacies. Uninsured patients in pilot states get a reliable $35-a-month supply channel.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is unusually well positioned for a drug-price measure: bipartisan sponsorship from 57 senators counting cosponsors, a favorable committee report, and a spot on the Senate calendar, with no recorded opposition. The most likely path is a Senate floor vote, possibly by unanimous consent, before the session ends January 3, 2027; but the Senate calendar is crowded, and even if the Senate passes it, enactment would require House action on a companion, which has not appeared in the record. Many calendar bills die at session's end for lack of floor time.
